title: The Book That Predicted Pete Hegseth’s Failures
gist: Keith Johnson uses the 50th anniversary of Norman F. Dixon's 'On the Psychology of Military Incompetence' as a diagnostic framework for Pete Hegseth's Pentagon, arguing the failure pattern is not stupidity but a self-selecting authoritarian, anti-innovation, anti-effeminacy mindset. The concrete indictments: the Pentagon failed to prepare for Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz despite decades of war-gaming, and four years after Ukraine proved the drone era the U.S. still lags Ukraine in drone output while Trump spurned Kyiv's drone assistance and funds a 'Trump-class' battleship.

themes.theme: Dixon's framework: incompetence as selection effect, not stupidity

insights.claim: Norman F. Dixon explicitly rules out stupidity as the root cause of military incompetence, noting many catastrophic commanders such as Douglas Haig were academic high achievers, and instead locates the cause in a mindset attracted to military institutions that the institutions then amplify by design.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: A reusable model for diagnosing institutional failure anywhere: screen for selection and promotion criteria, not for individual IQ.
insights.locator: Dixon rules out pure stupidity as a root cause

insights.claim: Dixon's core mechanism is that organizations promote people for traits—physical prowess over book smarts, love of tradition, spit-and-polish, petty rules—that are useless or catastrophic precisely at the highest ranks where those people end up.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: The generalizable warning: any promotion ladder that rewards conformity signals will systematically misplace leadership at the moment judgment matters most.
insights.quote: eventually the highest, precisely to positions where those characteristics were either useless or catastrophic
insights.locator: By and large, the (British) military shunned innovation

insights.claim: Dixon identifies an ingrained fear of 'effeminacy' that extended even to battlefield behavior—disdain for taking cover, wearing protective gear, and running protective convoys for merchant shipping in wartime—showing masculinity anxiety directly producing casualties.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Cultural signaling inside a force has measurable operational cost; a live test is whether current U.S. force-protection and convoy doctrine is being shaped by optics.
insights.locator: Another characteristic Dixon found in decades of military dysfunction

insights.claim: Dixon found that incompetent senior military leaders consistently shared an inability to tolerate criticism of any sort and a preference for subordinates whose loyalty outweighed their competence.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Loyalty-over-competence staffing is an observable, early-warning indicator of coming operational failure—applicable to corporate and political organizations alike.
insights.locator: Other constant characteristics among incompetent senior military leaders

insights.claim: Dixon argues authoritarian mindsets produce rigidity of thought that makes leaders less likely to understand enemy intentions and prone to underestimating enemy capability.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Predicts systematic threat underestimation—the single most expensive category of intelligence failure and the one hardest to price in advance.
insights.quote: Authoritarians will be less likely to understand enemy intentions

insights.claim: Dixon's own conclusion is inverted from the diagnosis: the traits of successful commanders are creativity, openness to new ideas and dissent, overcoming petty conventions and regulations, promoting the best and brightest, and embracing the unconventional.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Gives a positive checklist for evaluating military or executive leadership quality rather than only a failure taxonomy.
insights.locator: Yet it is still a fascinating glimpse at why the very things

insights.claim: The author concedes Dixon's book is dated in both case studies and science—heavy on Freudian mommy issues and Victorian public school trauma—and that newer scholarship recasts World War I British generals as a nearly competent class struggling with an entirely new way of war rather than as 'donkeys.'
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: A rare self-limiting caveat: the framework's explanatory power may be overfitted, so treat the Hegseth mapping as analogy rather than proof.
insights.locator: Dixon’s book is dated, both in its martial case studies

themes.theme: Strait of Hormuz: the war-gamed failure that happened anyway

insights.claim: The Pentagon failed to prepare for Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz despite the scenario having been war-gamed out for decades beforehand.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: The most consequential energy-supply chokepoint in the world was closed by an adversary the U.S. had modeled for decades—evidence that planning capacity does not translate into preparedness under current leadership.
insights.locator: today it reads as if he was writing about the Pentagon’s failure

insights.claim: Hegseth has been unable to subdue a third-rate country despite commanding history's most awesome military, according to the author's characterization of the ongoing Iran war.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Capability-to-outcome gap in a live conflict is the clearest real-time evidence for the incompetence thesis and a factor in how long the oil disruption persists.
insights.locator: Yet, it is impossible to read the book today

insights.claim: Hegseth's Pentagon purged the professional press corps and banished it from the building, rewrites casualty totals on a whim, and has not held a press briefing during wartime for nearly three months.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Official U.S. war data is now unreliable, forcing investors and analysts onto open-source and third-party sources for conflict assessment.
insights.locator: Like Dixon’s incompetents, who shunned publicity of any sort

insights.claim: Hegseth publicly chided the press as 'unpatriotic' for objective war reporting and melted down when lawmakers said the U.S. failure in the Iran war was ultimately his responsibility.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Congressional criticism is already framing the Iran war as a leadership failure—raising the probability of a Hegseth departure as a political event.
insights.locator: When it comes to prickly skin, Hegseth ticks all of Dixon’s boxes

themes.theme: Drone gap and technological rejection at the top

insights.claim: More than four years after the Ukraine war demonstrated the need to reconfigure combat forces for the drone era, the United States still lags Ukraine—described as a middling and war-beset European country—by miles in drone output.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: The U.S. drone-production gap is the single clearest defense-industrial investment thesis and the clearest measure of Pentagon adaptation failure.
insights.locator: Authoritarians are also less likely to embrace technical innovations

insights.claim: Trump spurned Ukraine's offer of drone assistance during the initial phases of the Iran war, forgoing the most battle-tested drone expertise available at the moment the U.S. most needed it.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Political preference is overriding capability acquisition—a durable structural drag on U.S. drone catch-up regardless of budget levels.
insights.locator: Part of that is due to Hegseth’s boss

insights.claim: Trump has for years advocated returning to old steam-powered catapults on U.S. aircraft carriers and has forced the Pentagon to allocate billions of dollars toward the future construction of a Trump-class 'battleship.'
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Billions are being routed into an obsolete platform class—a concrete misallocation to track in defense budget lines against drone and munitions underfunding.
insights.locator: Trump is consistent in his disdain for technological advances

themes.theme: Hegseth as the 'bull' archetype in office

insights.claim: Hegseth summoned every senior U.S. military commander from around the world to attend in person a harangue about fat soldiers, long hair, and beards, and posts videos of himself doing physical training—behavior unusual for a secretary of defense with broader strategic responsibilities.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Attention allocation at the top of the Pentagon is a leading indicator of what does not get done—here, force modernization and theater planning.
insights.locator: Hegseth summoned every single senior U.S. military commander

insights.claim: Hegseth topped out as a major in the National Guard after tours in Iraq and Afghanistan and has carried a junior officer's mindset into the office of the secretary of defense.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: The rank-to-role mismatch is the author's structural explanation for tactical fixation displacing strategy at the top of the U.S. defense establishment.
insights.locator: Pete Hegseth is not a general

insights.claim: Hegseth is mandating testosterone tests and possible injections for U.S. 'warfighters' alongside a systematic bias against promoting female officers and expanding female combat troops, matching Dixon's diagnosis of masculinity anxiety driving personnel and force structure decisions.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Narrowing the recruitment and promotion pool during a manpower-strained war is a direct readiness cost, not merely a culture-war story.
insights.locator: Dixon’s belief that fears about masculinity drive some senior leaders’ behavior

insights.claim: Trump selected Hegseth for secretary of defense because he was straight out of 'central casting,' making appearance the explicit selection criterion for the top U.S. defense job—an exact instance of Dixon's preoccupation with outward appearances.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: If casting is the selection function for cabinet posts, expect the same failure pattern to recur across other agencies, not just defense.
insights.quote: he was picked for the job by President Donald Trump because Hegseth was straight out of “central casting.”
insights.locator: But then—he was picked for the job by President Donald Trump

insights.claim: U.S. military failure has traditionally been marked by chaotic arrogance rather than the spit-and-polish obsessions Dixon diagnosed in the British, making Hegseth's parade-ground fixation a foreign import into American institutional dysfunction.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Suggests the current failure mode is novel for the U.S. system, so historical American recovery patterns may not apply.
insights.locator: Yet traditionally, U.S. failure has been marked more by chaotic arrogance
